TCP 層的保活探測（手冊 §2.3.1 AT+QICFG=\"tcp/keep: TCP-layer keepalive probing (manual §2.3.1 AT+QICFG="tcp/keepalive"). ⚠ Against tcpbin.com's 15 s idle timeout it is "completely useless" — measured with keepalive on, the connection was still closed at 15.1 s: keepalive sends empty probe packets at the TCP layer, which the application never sees, while tcpbin counts "has any application data arrived"; and interval_time has a minimum of 25 s anyway, already longer than 15 s. The only way to survive an application-layer timeout is to send real data (for example a newline every 10 s with AT+QISENDEX=0,"0A"). Where it genuinely helps is "keeping the carrier's NAT mapping alive and detecting dead connections" — the NAT mapping of an IoT SIM is reclaimed after a few idle minutes, which is a disconnection at another level. The parameter ranges come from the manual; press QICFG=? to see the ranges this firmware actually reports (no traffic). ⚡ Traffic: the four QICFG commands "themselves" never touch the network (they only read and write module settings), but once keepalive is enabled, any socket that is open and idle makes the probe packets go out over the air for real and count against your mobile data. Estimate (the manual does not state the packet size; the figures below are derived from a standard TCP/IPv4 frame and are not a Quectel specification): one probe is a payload-free TCP segment of 20+20=40 bytes, the peer's ACK is another 40 bytes, so about 80 bytes per round trip. With the default idle=30 s and the connection staying idle throughout, that is 120 probes per hour × 80 bytes ≈ 9.4 KB, roughly 225 KB a day and 6.8 MB a month. ⚠ A prepaid SIM such as 1NCE has a finite total allowance, so raise the idle value if you leave it running long-term (for example 600 s → about 11 KB a day). With no socket open, no probe is sent at all and no data is used.
